scenes.text: Picture this. Overnight, your agents wrote forty changes to a billing system. All pass their tests. One changes what customers are charged. Who catches it? [pause] The tests? A person, reading all forty? Or a person, at a stop built for it? [pause] <emphasis>A stop built for it.</emphasis> Tests can't say whether you wanted the change. And nobody reads forty carefully.

scenes.text: So where does a person decide? A good rule of thumb is four questions. Does it move money? Does it touch customer data? Is it hard to undo? Is it a judgment call that no check can make? [pause] One yes, and a person decides. Four no's, and that kind of change can ship on its checks.

data.label: WHERE DOES A PERSON DECIDE?  ·  A RULE OF THUMB: FOUR QUESTIONS

verdicts.text: Four no’s: that kind of change can ship on its checks.

scenes.text: Take our made-up example: the subscription-billing system from lesson one. Overnight, an agent drafts six things. Fix a typo on an internal admin screen. Add a missing test for renewals. Four no's, both times. They ship on their checks, and nobody waits.

Change how a late fee is calculated
Migrate the ledger to a new schema
Send customer emails to a new partner

data.caption: Four no’s: nobody waits.

scenes.text: Change how a late fee is calculated. That moves money: the finance owner decides. [pause] Migrate the ledger. Money again, and hard to undo: the ledger's owner decides. [pause] Send customer emails to a new partner. Customer data: the data owner decides.

scenes.text: And it isn't only code. A refund over the limit: the agent prepares it, a support lead approves it. Under the limit, a person already decided, when they set it. [pause] Six pieces of work. Four stops. Two never waited.

scenes.text: A stop only works if a person can clear it quickly. So the agent doesn't hand over a wall of diff and ask, okay? It prepares the decision. What changes. Why. The evidence, from the pipeline: last month's invoices, recomputed, old against new. The risk. And the way back. [pause] Now the finance owner decides about the fee. And an engineer still reviews the code that moves money.

scenes.text: Then write it down: who approves what, in a file in the repository. Fees and prices: the finance owner. The ledger: its owner. The checks, the pipeline, and this file itself: always a person. Anything the list doesn't cover: stop and ask. [pause] And the pipeline enforces it, by what a change touches. The agent that wrote a change doesn't classify it, or approve it. An old idea from accounting: whoever prepares a payment doesn't approve it.

scenes.text: So, to recap. Design where people decide. Make every stop quick to clear. And let the rest ship on its checks, one released kind at a time.

scenes.text: Which gives us rule five, for your agents. Before a change ships, find out who decides. Money, customer data, hard to undo, or a judgment call: stop for the person named in the repo, and bring the change, the evidence, the risk, and the way back. Not on the list: stop and ask. Ship on checks alone only what a person has released.

scenes.text: Now, your turn. Give your A.I. the last ten changes to a system you run, and the four questions. Ask it: which of these needed a person? Which could have shipped on checks alone? [pause] Then see where you disagree.
